title: What is the difference between OLTP (row-oriented stores like PostgreSQL — fast single-row transactions) and OLAP (columnar stores like Redshift/BigQuery — fast aggregations over few columns), and why should you NOT run heavy analytics on your production OLTP database?
shortTitle: OLTP versus OLAP, and why not to run analytics on your OLTP database

s1_definition.profdef: OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems like PostgreSQL and MySQL are row-oriented stores optimized for many small, concurrent read/write transactions touching few rows each, with strong consistency and low latency. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) systems like Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake are column-oriented stores optimized for scanning and aggregating a few columns across billions of rows. Running heavy analytics on a production OLTP database competes for the same CPU, memory, buffer cache, and locks that serve live customer transactions, degrading both.
s1_definition.analogy: OLTP is the busy teller counter at the National Bank — thousands of quick deposits and withdrawals, each touching one account, needing to be fast and correct. OLAP is the analyst in the back room who asks "what was the total deposit volume across all branches for the last five years?" If you force the teller counter to also run that giant report, the queue freezes while the machine chews through billions of rows. You keep the two jobs on separate systems.
s1_definition.oneliner: OLTP serves fast single-row transactions; OLAP scans few columns across billions of rows — keep heavy analytics off your transactional database.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems like PostgreSQL and MySQL are row-oriented stores optimized for many small, concurrent read/write transactions touching few rows each, with strong consistency and low latency. OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) systems like Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake are column-oriented stores optimized for scanning and aggregating a few columns across billions of rows. Running heavy analytics on a production OLTP database competes for the same CPU, memory, buffer cache, and locks that serve live customer transactions, degrading both.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** OLTP is the busy teller counter at the National Bank — thousands of quick deposits and withdrawals, each touching one account, needing to be fast and correct. OLAP is the analyst in the back room who asks "what was the total deposit volume across all branches for the last five years?" If you force the teller counter to also run that giant report, the queue freezes while the machine chews through billions of rows. You keep the two jobs on separate systems.

**One line to remember:** OLTP serves fast single-row transactions; OLAP scans few columns across billions of rows — keep heavy analytics off your transactional database.

sections.s2_technical:
The core difference is physical storage layout. OLTP databases store data row by row: all columns of one account sit together on disk. This is perfect for a transaction like "read Rajesh's full account row, update his balance" because one small read or write touches one place. Indexes make finding that single row fast, and row locking keeps concurrent transactions correct.

OLAP databases store data column by column: all the `amount` values across millions of rows sit together, all the `txn_date` values sit together, and so on. This is perfect for "sum the amount column across five years" because the engine reads only the `amount` column — not the fifty other columns in each row — and compresses it heavily since similar values cluster. Columnar scans plus compression plus massive parallelism make aggregations over billions of rows fast.

Now consider why each is bad at the other's job. An OLAP columnar store is terrible at updating one account's balance, because a single logical row is scattered across many column files. An OLTP row store is terrible at summing one column across billions of rows, because it must read every full row, dragging in all the columns you did not want, and it has no columnar compression to help.

The reason you must not run heavy analytics on your production OLTP database is resource contention. That five-year aggregation will read a huge fraction of the table, evicting the hot pages that live transactions depend on from the buffer cache, so afterwards even fast transactions hit disk. It consumes CPU and memory that the teller traffic needs. It can hold shared locks or generate long-running snapshots that bloat the database. The result is exactly the connection-pool and latency cascade where one heavy query slows everything.

The standard architecture separates the two. Writes and live reads go to the OLTP primary. Data is then replicated or ETL'd into an OLAP warehouse — through change-data-capture, nightly batch loads, or streaming pipelines — where analysts run their heavy queries without touching production. A lighter middle ground is a read replica of the OLTP database for moderate reporting, but true heavy analytics belong in a columnar warehouse. This separation also lets each system scale independently and use the storage format suited to its workload.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the live transfer system runs on PostgreSQL and serves thousands of small transfers per second. This is exactly what OLTP is for — fast, correct, single-account transactions.

Problem 2 — The finance team starts running a "total deposits by month across five years" report directly against PostgreSQL during business hours, and the teller app slows to a crawl. This is exactly why you do not run analytics on OLTP — the report scans the whole table, evicts hot pages, and starves live traffic.

Problem 3 — We move the heavy aggregation into a columnar warehouse fed by change-data-capture, so analysts query there while PostgreSQL stays fast for customers. This is exactly the OLTP/OLAP separation.

We will build a `TransferService` for the OLTP path and an `AnalyticsService` that queries the warehouse (represented by a separate datasource), plus a CDC-style exporter concept, so the two workloads never compete.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
banking-platform/
├── oltp-service/
│   └── src/main/java/com/bank/oltp/
│       ├── service/TransferService.java
│       └── model/Account.java
├── analytics-service/
│   └── src/main/java/com/bank/analytics/
│       └── service/AnalyticsService.java
└── resources/
    ├── oltp-application.yml
    └── olap-application.yml
```

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- OLTP (PostgreSQL) — row store, fast single-row writes
CREATE TABLE accounts (
    account_id  VARCHAR(20) PRIMARY KEY,
    holder_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
    balance     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL
);

-- OLAP (Redshift/BigQuery) — columnar, fast aggregation.
-- In Redshift you choose column encodings and a sort/dist key.
CREATE TABLE fact_transactions (
    txn_date   DATE,
    account_id VARCHAR(20),
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2),
    txn_type   VARCHAR(10)
)
DISTSTYLE KEY DISTKEY (account_id)
SORTKEY (txn_date);

-- Heavy aggregation that belongs on OLAP, NOT on the OLTP primary:
-- SELECT date_trunc('month', txn_date) AS m, SUM(amount)
-- FROM fact_transactions WHERE txn_type='DEPOSIT'
-- GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# oltp-application.yml — live transactions
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://oltp-primary:5432/bankdb
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20
---
# olap-application.yml — analytics warehouse (separate system)
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:redshift://warehouse.cluster:5439/analytics
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 5   # few, long-running analytical queries
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# OLTP service (live traffic)
mvn -pl oltp-service clean package
java -jar oltp-service/target/oltp-service.jar --spring.config.location=resources/oltp-application.yml

# Analytics service (warehouse) — separate deployment, separate datasource
mvn -pl analytics-service clean package
java -jar analytics-service/target/analytics-service.jar --spring.config.location=resources/olap-application.yml

# Data pipeline: CDC from PostgreSQL → warehouse (e.g. Debezium → Kafka → loader)
# Analysts query the warehouse; the OLTP primary stays fast for customers.
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: thousands of live transfers per second plus one five-year deposit report.

Step 1: A transfer arrives. `TransferService` runs two tiny single-row updates on the PostgreSQL primary. Because PostgreSQL stores each account as a contiguous row, the update touches one small place and commits in milliseconds.

Step 2: Change-data-capture reads the write-ahead log of these committed changes and streams them into a pipeline. The live database is not queried by analytics at all.

Step 3: The pipeline loads the changes into the columnar warehouse's `fact_transactions` table. Here the `amount`, `txn_date`, and `txn_type` columns are stored separately and compressed.

Step 4: The finance team runs the monthly deposit aggregation via `AnalyticsService`, which points at the warehouse. The columnar engine reads only the `amount`, `txn_date`, and `txn_type` columns across billions of rows, in parallel, and returns monthly totals.

Step 5: Throughout the heavy report, the OLTP primary's buffer cache stays warm with live account pages, so teller transactions remain fast. The two workloads never compete because they live on separate systems with storage layouts suited to each.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:50 INFO  TransferService - OLTP transfer 50000 from SAV2001 to CUR3001
2026-10-25 13:50:51 INFO  AnalyticsService - Running 5-year deposit aggregation on the OLAP warehouse
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  LIVE TRAFFIC (OLTP)                         ANALYTICS (OLAP)
  ┌──────────────┐                            ┌───────────────────┐
  │ Teller / App │                            │ Finance analysts  │
  └──────┬───────┘                            └─────────┬─────────┘
         │ small single-row txns                        │ heavy aggregations
         ▼                                              ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐   CDC (WAL) → Kafka   ┌───────────────────────┐
  │ PostgreSQL (row) │══════════════════════▶│ Redshift/BigQuery      │
  │ accounts         │   nightly/stream load │ fact_transactions      │
  │ fast writes      │                       │ columnar + compressed  │
  └──────────────────┘                       │ scans FEW columns      │
   buffer cache stays warm                   │ over BILLIONS of rows  │
   for live transactions                     └───────────────────────┘

 Do NOT run the 5-year SUM on PostgreSQL — it evicts hot pages,
    burns CPU, and freezes the teller queue.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Two Services, Two Stores ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ──────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: TransferService = writes; AnalyticsService = reads   │
  │ D: each depends on its OWN datasource abstraction       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │       TransferService         │   │       AnalyticsService         │
  │ - oltp: JdbcTemplate (PG)     │   │ - olap: JdbcTemplate (Redshift)│
  │ @Transactional                │   │ (read-only, long queries)      │
  │ + transfer(from,to,amount)    │   │ + monthlyDepositTotals(): List │
  │   single-row UPDATEs          │   │   SUM over few columns         │
  └───────────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────────┘

  Storage layout:
    OLTP row:  [SAV2001 | Rajesh | 1,000,000 | ACTIVE]  ← one read = one txn
    OLAP col:  amount:   [50000, 25000, 70000, ...]     ← scan one column
               txn_date: [2024-03-01, 2024-03-01, ...]  ← compressed

  Contract:
    OLTP: fast single-row, strong consistency, low latency
    OLAP: fast aggregation over billions, eventually-consistent copy
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
OLTP and OLAP differ fundamentally in how they store data on disk. OLTP databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL are row-oriented: all the columns of one account sit together, which is perfect for a transaction that reads or updates a single account's row quickly and correctly under heavy concurrency. OLAP databases like Redshift, BigQuery, and Snowflake are column-oriented: all the values of one column sit together and are heavily compressed, which is perfect for scanning and aggregating a few columns across billions of rows.

Each is deliberately bad at the other's job. A columnar store is poor at updating one account's balance because a single logical row is scattered across many column files. A row store is poor at summing one column across billions of rows because it must read every full row, dragging in all the columns you did not ask for, with no columnar compression to help.

You must not run heavy analytics on your production OLTP database because of resource contention. A five-year aggregation reads a huge fraction of the table, evicts the hot pages that live transactions depend on from the buffer cache, burns the CPU and memory the live traffic needs, and can hold long-running snapshots that bloat the database. The result is that your fast customer transactions suddenly hit disk and the whole system slows — one heavy query dragging everything down. The correct architecture keeps writes and live reads on the OLTP primary and replicates or ETLs the data into a columnar warehouse through change-data-capture or batch pipelines, where analysts run their heavy queries without ever touching production.

At the National Bank of India, the finance team began running a five-year monthly deposit report directly against our PostgreSQL primary during business hours, and the teller application slowed to a crawl because the report scanned the whole table and evicted the live account pages from cache. I moved that workload into a columnar warehouse fed by change-data-capture, so analysts query the warehouse while PostgreSQL stays fast for customers. The line I always keep in mind is that OLTP serves fast single-row transactions and OLAP scans few columns over billions of rows, so I keep heavy analytics off the transactional database.
